title: ISSR: Iterative Selection with Self-Review for Vocabulary Test Distractor Generation
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically generating high-quality distractors for English vocabulary multiple-choice test items. The authors focus on the challenge of using large language models (LLMs) to support teachers in building vocabulary assessments without producing distractors that accidentally create multiple correct answers. The study asks whether LLMs can directly generate distractors effectively and how a system can validate distractors so that only one answer remains correct.

To address this, the paper proposes the ISSR framework (Iterative Selection with Self-Review), which combines a pretrained language model candidate generator, an LLM-based distractor selector, and an LLM-based distractor validator. The framework first generates many candidate distractors, filters them using rules derived from analysis of exam items, then asks an LLM to select plausible distractors and uses a self-review mechanism to remove distractors that could also function as correct answers. The empirical work evaluates distractor-generation quality against teacher-designed distractors from Taiwan’s General Scholastic Ability Test (GSAT) English exam.

The population and context are Taiwanese high school students indirectly represented through archival exam data, along with teachers as the intended end users of the system. The dataset consists of English vocabulary questions from the GSAT, a university entrance exam used with senior high school students in Taiwan. The study is not a classroom intervention and does not test effects on students’ reading or vocabulary learning outcomes; instead, it analyzes item characteristics and benchmarks automated distractor generation methods on exam questions.

The main conclusion is that direct LLM generation of distractors is unstable and weaker than a structured pipeline. ISSR outperforms baseline approaches for generating distractors that better match human-designed exam items, and the self-review mechanism helps filter invalid distractors. However, the paper also notes limitations in computing cost, speed, dependence on the quality of the candidate set, and limited generalizability beyond the GSAT context.
quality_tier_rationale: This is primarily a technical preprint evaluating NLP/distractor-generation performance on exam items, not a randomized or strong quasi-experimental study of student learning. It provides no direct causal classroom evidence and no K-12 intervention-outcome design meeting the framework's credibility criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising technical performance for assessment authoring support, but impact on learners or teachers in authentic educational settings is unclear and unmeasured. For the user's target topic, it should be treated as adjacent evidence rather than evidence of reading impact.

interventions.use_case: LLM-supported generation and validation of distractors for English vocabulary multiple-choice test design, aimed at helping teachers construct EFL vocabulary assessments.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the ISSR framework outperformed baseline distractor-generation approaches on automatic distractor generation benchmarks for English vocabulary test design, suggesting improved support for teacher item creation. Reported metrics include F1@3=1.55%, F1@10=2.07%, NDCG@3=3.57%, NDCG@10=6.31%, and NDCG@30=9.82% for ISSR versus lower scores for CDGP and direct GPT-based generation/selection; however, no classroom productivity, time-saved, or teacher-use outcomes were directly measured.
finding.measure: Automatic distractor-generation benchmark metrics (F1@k, NDCG@k) for vocabulary test item design
finding.study_size: n=195 exam questions total; 193 test questions in main experiments

finding.finding_summary: Although the system targets English vocabulary assessment design, the paper does not test whether use of ISSR improves student reading, vocabulary, decoding, fluency, or comprehension outcomes. Evidence is limited to item-generation performance on Taiwan university entrance exam vocabulary questions, so there is no direct causal or classroom evidence for foundational reading outcomes in K-12 settings.
finding.measure: No direct student literacy outcome measured; proxied only by exam-item/distractor generation quality
finding.study_size: n=195 exam questions total; no student intervention sample
